## 1. The World of Heraldry

*Banners rot in the rain. Shrines sink into the mud. Oaths are broken, kings are buried, and the roads between settlements grow more dangerous with each passing season. Yet the ruins of the world still glitter with coin, relics, and forgotten power, and the desperate, the devout, the greedy, and the doomed continue to march into darkness to claim them.*

### 1.1 What is Heraldry Skirmish?

**Heraldry Skirmish** is a competitive GM-less PvPvE fantasy tabletop miniatures game of desperate expeditions, brutal clashes, and hard-won survival. Most battles pit two rival adventuring parties against one another as they race through monster-haunted ruins, damned wilderness, and blood-soaked strongholds in search of treasure, glory, and escape.

A standard competitive game uses **4 Heroes per side** on a **36"×36"** battlefield. It is usually played by **2 players**, but supports **2–8 players** by dividing control of each side's Heroes among allied players.

The battlefield is never passive. Neutral Monsters stalk the field, hazards punish hesitation, and scenarios place pressure on both sides from the first activation to the last. Even victory is rarely clean. The party that leaves the field richest is often the one that bled for every coin.

Heraldry Skirmish supports **solo** and **cooperative** play. In those games, **1–4 players** control **1–4 allied Heroes** against scenarios strengthened by additional Monsters, harsher threats, and fixed PvE pressure in place of a rival party. Whether played competitively or cooperatively, Heraldry is built around dangerous choices, concise tactical rules, and the constant risk that boldness will be rewarded before it is punished.

A typical single game, called an adventure, lasts about 60–90 minutes (4–8 rounds). A typical campaign spans 16–18 adventures and is usually split across 8–18 play sessions.

Use the routes below to learn or reference the game. The table is a navigation aid only and does not replace or modify the cited rules.

| Goal | Recommended route |
| --- | --- |
| **First game** | Use **Appendix A. Learn to Play**; it contains the complete first-game setup, fixed parties, scenario, and guided opening. After it, create a standard party and choose any Core Scenario marked **[Intro]** for your first adventure using the full rules. |
| **Quick or demonstration game** | Use **Appendix B. Basic Mode**; consult the full core rules or **Appendix C** when Basic Mode directs you there. |
| **Standard one-off adventure** | Begin with **2. Core Mechanics**, then read the sections required by the chosen Heroes and scenario. Keep **Appendix C. Rules Reference** available during play. |
| **Campaign** | Use the standard-play route, then read **11. Campaign Play** before creating the campaign record or beginning the first campaign adventure. |
| **Rules lookup during play** | Start with **Appendix C** and follow its cited full-rule section when more detail is required. |

A **Hero** is a player-controlled adventurer and the main unit of campaign progression. A **Hireling** is an allied non-Hero combatant controlled by a party. A **Monster** is a neutral or hostile non-party combatant controlled by Monster AI. A **Summon** is a temporary combatant that their creating rule identifies as a Summon.

### 1.2 The Grim World

*The world of **Heraldry Skirmish** is a realm of old faiths, broken kingdoms, hungry roads, and cold bargains. Kings, princes, bishops, and warlords still raise banners over land they can barely hold. They fight over relics, tolls, doctrine, trade roads, salt, iron, and pride. Their victories are measured in burnt farms and new taxes. Their defeats are carried by peasants who never chose a side.*

*Most people live close to a gate. A palisade, a bell, a chapel lamp, and a few armed neighbours are the shape of civilization now. Beyond them lie drowned fields, plague roads, ruined shrines, black forests, dead bridges, and the shattered works of older realms. Merchants who travel between holdings are not soft clerks with ledgers. They bargain, lie, fight, navigate, and plan funerals with equal care. They know which inns change names too often. They know which milestones bleed in rain.*

*The countryside has teeth. Bandits prey on the weak and call it tax. Beasts prowl where the ploughs stopped. Goblin raiders descend on lonely roads and isolated farms. Orcs, gnolls, and kobolds test the borderlands for weakness and plunder. Haunted crypts and mass graves fill with the failures of earlier expeditions. The dead do not always stay down. Some rise hungry. Some rise bitter. Some rise with orders still clenched behind their teeth.*

*Beneath ruined towers, sunken monasteries, and collapsed fortresses lie the vaults of fallen empires. Coin waits there. Relics wait there. Forbidden lore waits there too, written in dust, iron, blood, and languages that make candles gutter. Dragons still brood in the deep places of the earth and on the high forgotten peaks. Their hoards could ransom kingdoms. Their wrath could end them.*

*Magic is real, feared, and never trusted. It is too common to dismiss and too dangerous to treat as ordinary. Curses, omens, failed workings, and old catastrophes have taught peasants to spit before speaking of it. Wizards dig power from broken observatories, dust-choked books, and stolen manuscripts. Sorcerers pay in blood for gifts they rarely understand. Priests beg miracles from distant powers that answer by silence as often as grace. Druids bargain with roots, rivers, storms, and things that remember the world before walls. Psions return from forbidden disciplines with minds cracked open and something still echoing inside.*

*Sensible people cling to hearth, habit, and walls. Your **Heroes** do not. They take writs from patrons who will not bleed for their own promises. They cross causeways where relief columns vanished, ford rivers that carry bones in flood season, and pry gold from rooms that should have stayed shut. In Heraldry, glory is a rumour told after the bodies are counted. Survival is a debt renewed one Skirmish at a time.*

### 1.3 The Dying Lands

**The Dying Lands at a Glance.** One ruined continent, six climates: the overgrown **Greenmark**, the ash-choked **Ashlands**, the lightless **Undermarches**, the frozen **Pale City**, the sun-scorched **Sun-Drowned**, and **The Mire**, poisoned and drowning beneath its own waters. Six **Bastions** hold what remains of mortal civilization; everything between them belongs to the dead and to the old powers that waited out the Fall. Adventurers are the few who go out into that country anyway. The sections below tell the story. The rules begin at **1.4**.

*The world has fallen. The old roads end at graves. The horizon belongs to the things beyond the walls now.*

*The lands where Heraldry Skirmish is fought are not a kingdom. They are a continent in the oldest sense: a single body of land held together by mountains, rivers, roads, ruins, and grief long after its crowns and borders stopped being useful.*

*Six ruined climates define the known world. Each one keeps its own weather, customs, hungers, and dead. Forest has taken the old roads. Ash cities still enforce their laws. The deep places have opened under mines and cellars. The north is locked in a winter that will not spend itself. The southern dunes grind palaces into salt and bone. The marshes rise each year and return what they swallowed changed.*

*Mortal civilization survives behind walls. Six great holdings have endured into the present age. Villages, fortified keeps, shrine-forts, and palisaded hamlets huddle in their shadows. Each great holding is called a **Bastion**. The country between them belongs to the dead, the hungry, and the old powers that waited out the Fall. Adventurers are the few who march into that country and pretend the contract matters.*

#### 1.3.1 The Fall

*No one agrees on what ended the world. That has not stopped anyone from blaming someone else.*

*Priests preach withdrawal. The gods, they say, turned their faces away after a final insult no surviving scripture will name. The faithful inherited punishment without inheritance, guilt without proof, and chapel bells that still ring when no hand pulls the rope.*

*Wizards prefer catastrophe. They write of a working too large for mortal hands, an imperial formula that tore a seam in the unseen structure of the world. Everything since, they claim, is the slow widening of that wound. Druids speak of an oath broken beneath the roots. They say the poison went deeper than any grave. Sorcerers whisper that a bloodline opened like a door and let in what had always pressed from the other side. Psions describe a hammering under the ruins. They say every mind hears one splinter of the blow. A few scholars, reading the oldest crypt-songs, blame a shape with wings. They are not invited to preach.*

*The common folk have stopped asking for one story. They use the names that fit the grief in front of them: **The Burning**, **The Long Silence**, **The Hollow Year**, **The Last Banner**, **The Drowning of the Throne**. Historians still argue the date. They argue the calendar first. Old people count generations since the Fall. Young people count winters since the last village they remember became empty.*

*What remains is easier to prove. The roads between old capitals are closed to honest travel. The great libraries are ash, sealed, flooded, or staffed by hands that no longer need blood. Harvests shrink on every coast that still deserves the name. Each season, some Bastion sends a relief column through a gate at dawn. By dusk the clerks are already leaving space for the column in the dead books.*

*The world is not dying gently. It dies like a wounded animal under a hedge. Slow. Aware. Dangerous to touch.*

#### 1.3.2 The Six Climates of Ruin

*Beyond the walls, land has become allegiance. Expedition ledgers still say forest, city, cavern, ice, desert, and swamp. Survivors know better. They use older names. The shape of the world is plain enough to anyone who has walked it. The broken mountains run down its spine. The dead empire and its ruined cities sprawl across the eastern heart. The great forest spreads west to the sea, the ice locks the north, the dunes burn in the south beyond the mountain passes, and the swamps drown the south-east where the rivers give out at the sea. The old imperial roads still join all of it, straight and patient, running out from the Ashlands to every climate that survived. A dry label cannot warn a traveller that a road has memory, a court still sits without lungs, or a pool of black water may be listening.*

##### The Greenmark

*The Greenmark is the great temperate forest of the surviving world. It is larger than the maps. Roots take a road within a season and make the milestones useless. Travellers report trees shifting at the edge of sight, upright hounds between trunks, and grove-circles where moss stays warm after snow. Foresters cut warning signs into bark for those who know how to read them. The most common sign means turn back even if the voice ahead is your own. The forest is no wilderness. It is a country that does not recognize human law.*

##### The Ashlands

*The Ashlands are the cities of the old empires after fire, law, and death finished with them. They sprawl across the eastern heart of the world, where the imperial roads still run out to every climate like spokes from a shattered wheel. Forums have collapsed into crypts. Temples lean over plazas filled with soot. Streets run black across districts no living guide will enter twice. Lamps still burn in shrines whose gods have no congregation. Patrols still cross boundaries that vanished before the current Bastions had names. The Ashlands are rich because whole treasuries died under stone. They are feared because the city still knows how to count.*

##### The Undermarches

*The Undermarches begin under every place that claims to have a foundation, and run deepest beneath the broken mountains at the world's centre. Mines break into older shafts. Older shafts open into tunnels no pick made. Surveyors return with maps that disagree with themselves. Webs thick as rope choke the lower galleries, and the miners who cut them do not ask what spun them. Wells sour overnight. Cellars breathe in winter. Borders on the surface mean little below, where passages run under rivers, burial hills, and walls the Bastions call secure. Down in the true dark the deep elves keep their own houses and their own law, older than any empire and crueller than any court that ever sat above. The deep does not need to invade. The surface keeps falling into it.*

##### The Pale City

*In the north, winter has become government. Cities that once held tens of thousands stand ice-locked, their gates frozen mid-closing. Towers crack in the cold. The **White Court** still sits, its dead nobility frozen in order of precedence, and its offices, processions, and taxes continue in forms no living citizen would recognize. Hearthhold sends parties north with oil, fire-charms, and instructions to leave tribute on the old road. No one agrees who first made that bargain. The snow covers ruin with clean hands. It heals nothing.*

##### The Sun-Drowned

*South of the broken mountains, the dunes have climbed over the wealthiest realms the world ever boasted. Tomb-cities of the priest-kings break the horizon like teeth. Salt flats glitter where harbours stood. The desert leaves the dead in sight, enthroned, armoured, embalmed, or half-uncovered by wind. Saltspire's ledgers call the southern routes profitable. Its guides call them damned and charge for the difference. Under the sand, sealed courts keep their lamps lit, and the greatest of the priest-kings, the **Sun-Crowned Prince**, has not yet been told that their reign is over.*

##### The Mire

*Where the southern rivers gave out before the sea, the swamps inherited the rest, spreading across the world's south-eastern lowlands. Bogs swallowed roads. Mangroves grew through village roofs. Stilt-houses lean over water that looks shallow until it opens. Reedmarch survives by toll, ferry, leechcraft, and denial. The hag-courts hold the deep fen, and they keep older bargains than any Bastion will admit to honouring. Bells toll under the black water at the fen's heart, and every stilt-village knows the day its tribute falls due. Everyone there knows The Mire is rising. No one profits from saying it aloud. The dead drift below the walkways. Sometimes they drift back.*

*These six are the world now. The Bastions are what mortal civilization built against them. They are also what mortal civilization hides inside.*

#### 1.3.3 The Six Bastions

*Each **Bastion** is a fortified holding: a walled town, a fortress-chapel, a sealed mining city, a stilt-town behind its toll-chains. None ruled before the Fall. They survived because they were small enough to be missed, lucky enough to be spared, or stubborn enough to close the gate while neighbours screamed outside. Now they are the great powers of what remains.*

*The six Bastions are not the only places where people live. They are the only places strong enough to claim next year with a straight face. Each shelters a ring of lesser holdings: tributary villages, palisaded hamlets, watch-keeps, toll bridges, shrine-forts, and the petty fiefs of minor lords who lost their kingdoms when the world ended. These lesser rulers still call themselves kings, princes, bishops, and marshals. Their domains are often smaller than the gardens their grandparents once owned.*

*They quarrel over relics, doctrine, tariffs, road rights, borders, stolen grain, marriage debts, and insults preserved beyond reason. They quarrel less with the Bastion that lets them winter behind its walls.*

*The Bastions themselves are not allies. They send envoys. They trade iron, salt, grain, oil, bodies, medicine, and lies. They exchange prisoners when it is useful. They accept refugees when plague at the gate would be worse than charity. Their treaties are thin things. Tired clerks write them. Hungry captains break them. No Bastion can afford open war with another. No Bastion trusts that fact to last.*

*The Bastions are not safe. They are safer. Their walls keep out the worst of the dark, not hunger, fever, debt, politics, superstition, or the quiet passengers hidden among refugees and trade goods. Every gate has a price. Every chapel keeps lists. Every guild counts favours. Every watch-fire burns lower than the captains admit.*

*Life inside the walls is crowded and mean. Families sleep in stairwells. Old soldiers sell their wounds as credentials. Minor lords quarrel over streets they do not own. Priests bless children who may later be sent beyond the gates under chapel seal. Coin buys food, medicine, forgiveness, silence, and time. It does not buy innocence.*

*The gates do not ask what a refugee is. They ask whether the refugee can hold a spear. Humans are the most numerous and the least agreed on anything. Dwarves keep the forges, the cisterns, and the grudges. Halflings keep the kitchens, the back stairs, and half the smuggling. Elves and gnomes are suffered for what they remember and what they can repair. Goblins, orcs, and ratkin fill the lower wards, sworn to the gate that admitted them and trusted exactly as far as the last raid allows. Deep elves, demonborn, and drakeblood are rarer, and each carries a rumour heavier than their pack. Every Bastion counts all of them on the wall at night. By daylight it counts them differently.*

*For most people, the Bastion is the end of the world made habitable by walls. For adventurers, it is where wounds are priced, contracts are stamped, dead companions are replaced, and the next mistake is made official. The **Town Phase** is not peace. It is the part of the war fought with ledgers, knives, prayers, and closed doors.*

##### Greythorn

***Greythorn** is a timber-walled town among ancient oaks at the last surviving crossroads of the western forest road. It endures because it pays the forest. Each autumn, tithe-bundles are left at the standing stones. Each spring, the gate-wardens count the foresters who returned, then count the tools of those who did not.*

*The Council of Captains governs Greythorn: six veteran rangers, hunters, and timber-masters who take command by season. Its people are practical, wary, and patient with druids because practical people pay what keeps them alive. The lower district, called the Hollow Quarter, is kept for forest emissaries. Dryad ambassadors, satyr envoys, and stranger figures cross its bridges under truce. Once each winter, a robed figure with antlers is admitted through the west gate and permitted to speak only with the senior Captain.*

*Greythorn imports iron from Deepwarden and salt from Reedmarch. It pays both grudgingly. It has not exchanged ambassadors with Sablekeep in nine winters over the Watch's caster laws. Its chapel is small. Its arcane spire is smaller. Its training yard is the largest in the world.*

##### Sablekeep

***Sablekeep** is a fortified chapel-town built into the throat of a ruined imperial city, where the Ashlands meet the eastern edge of the forest and the old roads run straight on into the dead empire. It survives by burning. Consecrated braziers stand at every gate, bridge, and chapel window. They are never permitted to go out. The lower terraces rest on the bones of an older temple, and the bones are not all the right shape.*

*The **Sable Watch** rules Sablekeep, an order of warrior-priests who train every able adult in vigil duty. The Watch claims no kingdom and no king. Its highest title, the **Lord Vigilant**, is conferred for life by acclamation of the captains and may be revoked only by death.*

*The Watch demands custody of every relic recovered from the Ashlands and the registration of every caster beneath its banner. Refusal of either is treated as war in all but name. The Watch hates the Ashlands. It trains its young to march into them anyway.*

##### Deepwarden

***Deepwarden** is a sealed mining city carved into the foothills of the broken mountains. It survived the Fall by closing its great gate. Half the city was on the wrong side when it closed. The half that survived now lives in the upper terraces above what its people call simply **the Dark**.*

*Deepwarden is governed by the **Lantern Council**: mine masters, tunnel-priests, and forge-captains who meet in chambers without doors that can be barred from the outside. Each Council member carries a lantern of consecrated flame. A Council member whose lantern goes dark is considered to have resigned.*

*Deepwarden controls the best forges in the surviving world. It pays for that monopoly with hunger for grain, labour, timber, and safe routes to the other Bastions, none of which it fully trusts. Adventurers find work here readily. Most contracts include a clause explaining what to do if the contractor begins speaking in a voice that does not belong to them.*

##### Hearthhold

***Hearthhold** is a walled town in the high north, built around the **Great Hearth** that has burned without interruption since the Fall. If the Hearth goes out, Hearthhold dies: first the children, then the elderly, then everyone. Every resident takes a turn on the fire-watch. Children are taught to feed the flame before they are taught to read.*

*Hearthhold is ruled by the **Hearth Marshal**, who is in practice the captain of the fire-watch and in protocol the sovereign of the town. The current Marshal is the seventh in an unbroken line, each chosen from the senior watch-captains by lot. The chapel is a side-chamber of the Hearth itself. The training ground is the wall around it.*

*Hearthhold needs fuel, grain, and bodies for the watch. It pays with the only currency it still has in quantity: the relics, weapons, and frozen treasures its parties drag back from the Pale City. It is the smallest of the Bastions, the poorest, and the bravest.*

##### Saltspire

***Saltspire** is a tower-city built around a deep, sacred well at the centre of an oasis ringed by salt-pans and the bones of older cities. It has the only reliable water for a hundred miles. This makes it wealthy. It also makes it hated.*

*The **Well-Keepers** govern Saltspire, a hereditary order of priest-administrators who maintain the well, the cisterns, and the city's law. Their authority is unchallenged within the walls and meaningless outside them. The city's defence is contracted to desert nomads, mercenary captains, and free companies, who are often paid in water rights rather than coin.*

*Saltspire controls the water and sells it like sovereignty. Its prices are not negotiated. Its treaties assume thirst will settle every argument in time. The well-shaft below the city descends farther than anyone alive has measured. The Well-Keepers do not permit it to be sounded.*

##### Reedmarch

***Reedmarch** is a stilt-town raised over log pilings on a network of barges, ferry platforms, and toll bridges. It is the only crossing for thirty miles in any direction. Its people are ferrymen, smugglers, apothecaries, leech-tenders, and corpse-haulers. They know what is buried under their floors. They prefer not to discuss it.*

*The Marsh Council governs Reedmarch: five families who hold the ferry rights, salt-pan rights, leech-harvests, medicines, and bone-yard. The Council meets in a hall built on a barge that is repositioned before every meeting, on the theory that enemies can visit a hall in a known location. Decisions pass by silence. Any motion the Council does not refuse aloud is considered carried.*

*Reedmarch controls the southern marsh roads, the common medicine trade, and every smuggling route worth a name. It charges for all three and refuses to itemize. Its adventurers are the only ones in the world fluent in negotiating with hags.*

#### 1.3.4 Magic in the Dying Lands

*The Five Traditions all survived the Fall. None survived intact.*

***Arcane Spells** are the inheritance of the broken empires. Wizards seek ruined libraries, half-burned grimoires, observatories with cracked lenses, and silent towers where their predecessors are still slumped over their work. Most Bastions tolerate wizards because they are useful. Tolerance is not trust. Sablekeep requires registration. Greythorn pays enough to keep them polite. Deepwarden watches their shadows on tunnel walls. They are blamed whenever blame needs a shape.*

***Divine Prayers** answer fitfully. The old saints remain in chapel rolls, and a few still seem to listen. Most do not. Priests who can call down a working become famous. Fame makes them useful, feared, and watched. Some teach that prayers fail because the gods withdrew. Others teach that prayers fail because the faithful are not yet worthy. Both teachings recruit. Both can get people killed.*

***Druidic Rituals** are alive in a way the other traditions are not. The forests have grown stronger since the Fall, and so have the rivers, storms, roots, and old stones. Druids are welcomed in Greythorn, tolerated in Reedmarch, mistrusted in Saltspire, and hanged in Sablekeep when the Watch can catch them without starting a riot. Their oldest circles teach that the world is shedding what no longer fits. They do not promise that mortal civilization will survive the shedding.*

***Sorceries** are the cheapest power to fall into and the most feared. They run in bloodlines, surface in fevers, and answer before they are understood. They always take their price in blood. No Bastion registers sorcerers, because no Bastion wants a list of them. Sablekeep hangs them. The others look away and hope the affliction burns itself out. A sorcerer learns early to spend the gift in private and to keep moving, because power that arrives uninvited is rarely forgiven by the neighbours who watched it arrive.*

***Psychic Abilities** are rarer still, and worse understood. They wake in those who have spent too long near ruin-thinned places, and no one can tell true sight from madness, possession, or grief until the damage is done. The Bastions distrust psions on principle and use them anyway, quietly, the way one uses a cracked tool that still cuts. A psion seldom asks for the gift and is seldom thanked for it. Most learn to say nothing of what they hear in other people's heads.*

*Magic-infused items are rarest of all. Each one is a wonder, a terror, a property dispute, and a possible catastrophe. A sword with a saint's name on the fuller may save a hamlet. It may also prove the chapel that sold it was lying. A ring taken from a drowned tomb may heal a wound, sour a bloodline, or make the wearer dream in a language spoken under the world.*

#### 1.3.5 Monstrous Threats

*The **Monsters** of the Dying Lands are not scattered obstacles. They hold the world now. They keep roads closed, fields empty, shrines silent, and old borders meaningless. A village may vanish because of hunger, tax, fever, or weather. Outside the walls, those causes often have claws, banners, laws, or names.*

***The Restless Dead** rise from plague pits, battlefields, sealed crypts, mass graves, drowned roads, and execution fields. Many are hunger given a body. Others remember offices, titles, and grudges. The lich-kings of the Ashlands hold court with the courtesy of rulers and the patience of corpses. The **Forsaken**, the dead empire's last sworn company, still hold the lines they were given, and their captain has forgotten the war but not the oath. Beneath the rubble, mummified guards, animated armour, and gargoyle hosts still answer laws no living tongue remembers.*

***Goblinoids, kobolds, gnolls, and orcs** raid wherever they can find a foothold. Goblin clans and web-wrights haunt the Greenmark roads. Gnoll war-bands ride the Sun-Drowned surface under banners cured stiff by heat. Orcs test borderlands for weak gates, poor watch, and winter hunger. Kobolds vanish into drains, old mines, and foundation cracks. Some serve stolen banners from older kingdoms. Some serve nothing. Some Bandit Captains of the forest roads are no longer mortal enough for that title to comfort anyone.*

***Beasts and corrupted beasts** prowl where settlement failed. Wolves follow armies that no longer march. Hounds walk upright between trees. Rime-beasts hunt broken northern streets. Carrion birds perch on standing stones and watch the living as if waiting for permission. Boars root in grave mould. Things with too many eyes weave roads shut in the Greenmark. Hydras patrol The Mire's channels. Shambling mounds and worse rise when the wet months come.*

***The old peoples and border powers** have not vanished. Were-creatures, satyr cohorts, dryad ambassadors, deep elves, nagas, gnoll raiders, necromancers, lizardfolk temple-guards, and stranger courts hold places the Bastions still mark as lost. Some bargain. Some tithe. Some raid. Some remember treaties humanity has forgotten and punish the breach with perfect sincerity. In the Sun-Drowned, the tomb-cities of the priest-kings are administered by **necromancers** who have outlasted their own deaths: judges, clerks, and tax-collectors preserved in linen, oil, and old authority. They do not acknowledge the Fall. They acknowledge overdue accounts.*

***Dragons** did not sleep easily through the Fall. Some woke into a world without tribute and decided to take it back. Others changed after feeding on what fell from the burning sky, what leaked from broken vaults, or what the dead left behind. Five named dragons mark the climate maps of the Dying Lands: **Maelthorn the Verdant** of the Greenmark, **Sirrach the Black** of the Undermarches, **Visath the White** of the Pale City, **Khorrun the Dracolich** of the Sun-Drowned, and **Vossegar of the Flooded Cathedral** in The Mire. No named dragon marks the Ashlands. The tales of the old cities claim their founders slew the region's dragons aeons before the Fall, raising capitals where hoards had cooled and bones had been divided into civic relics. Ashland courts disagree on how many dragons died. They agree only that the debt was paid in full, and that nothing winged has laid claim to the ash cities since. The oldest crypt-songs speak of a sixth, older than the Fall and perhaps its cause, which no map dares to mark. The wise do not say its name.*

*Khorrun alone among the five has not drawn breath since the Fall. Their bones still hold the shape of greed. The priest-king tombs they claimed were already full of the dead when they arrived, and the dead were glad of the company. Adventurers who have returned from Khorrun's vault describe a dragon-shaped absence at its centre, a hollow of lightning-scorched ribs, and ledgers stacked to the ceiling in every chamber, each recording exactly who has taken what, in handwriting no living scribe would claim. Parties do not hunt the five. They plan around them, as they plan around winter or plague. The **Avatar of the Old Growth**, said to walk in the deep Greenmark, is older than any of them and less interested in negotiation. Those who went looking for the Avatar were lost or came back unable to speak.*

***Demons, devils, cinder lords, frost bailiffs, and the unnamed** appear where sorcery has worn the world thin. They bargain more often than they kill. That makes them worse. Saltspire keeps a contract clerk whose only duty is to review infernal documents pressed on the city by passing envoys of fire and ash. The Pale City has courts where frost bailiffs conduct trials over warmth, trespass, and debts no living magistrate would recognize.*

***Imperial constructs and the wakeful dead of old empires** still patrol routes that no longer exist. They enforce decrees no living person can read. They answer to seals nobody now possesses. Some can be delayed by adventurers who know the correct titles. Most cannot be reasoned with at all.*

#### 1.3.6 Adventurers and the Road

*Adventurers exist because the Bastions need work done beyond the reach of soldiers.*

*A Bastion can fund armies for siege, garrisons for walls, and watch companies for gates. It cannot keep a standing army alive in the country between Bastions. Columns need wagons, fodder, road crews, messengers, surgeons, priests, and graves. The Greenmark returns regiments as antlers and boot leather. The Ashlands add their names to old rolls. The Undermarches take scouts through floors that were solid yesterday. The Pale City counts soldiers into its census. The Sun-Drowned lets thirst do the killing. The Mire waits for the road to sink beneath the baggage train.*

*What works is a party of four. Small enough to hide. Strong enough to fight. Cheap enough to lose.*

*So the patrons of every Bastion pay parties to do what armies cannot. Merchant houses chasing a debt, chapels hungry for relics, councils short of grain, debt-holders calling in what they are owed, Well-Keepers, watch captains, and discreet nobles all stamp writs and call them necessity. Each wants two things, the one written on the seal and the one that is not, and a wise party reads for both. Recover medicine from a ruined apothecary. Extract a relic from a sealed crypt and carry it to the chapel that will pay to register it. Burn a sorcerer out of a tower. Carry a sealed letter through The Mire to a holding that may not still be there. Recover a body before it can rise, or before a rival can. Slay a particular **Monster**. Confirm that another party did not. Each contract is a tax someone is willing to pay to keep their walls standing a little longer.*

*Parties take these contracts for different reasons. Some believe in the chapel, the council, the saint, the old oath, or the cause printed on the seal. Some take the coin and forget the cause before the gate closes behind them. Most take the work because starvation inside the walls is slower than danger outside them, and less likely to make a song.*

*Every Bastion knows rival parties work the same ruins. Rivalry is accounted for in the contracts. A council may hire one party to recover a strongbox and another to make sure no rival Bastion receives it. A chapel may bless both sides by mistake or policy. A noble may issue a warrant so old that nobody remembers whether the land named in it still exists. The Dying Lands settle such disputes without appeal.*

*Those who survive begin to build something larger than a purse. A keep on a hill. A reclaimed manor. A forge, a chapel, a vault, and a wall thick enough to last one hard winter. Few parties live long enough to raise such a place. Fewer reach **Triumph**, the old Bastion word for planting a banner in ground that has stayed clean for a generation. Every party leaving the gate tells itself this is the road ahead. Most roads end before that.*

#### 1.3.7 Legends and Echoes

*The Dying Lands remember. They do not remember kindly.*

***Saint Cael of the Broken Gate** held a river crossing during the first winter after the Fall while the dead crossed in the thousands. Cael ordered the refugees behind them to burn the bridge while Cael still stood on it. The Sable Watch teaches that Cael smiled as the fire took them. Older songs say they screamed and damned every god by name. Both versions are useful.*

***Ysolde Vane** was a witch-scholar who proved that some Arcane formulae could be strengthened by writing them in the caster's own blood. They were condemned by three courts, pardoned by two princes, and finally drowned in a locked iron cage. Their body was never recovered. Their marginalia still appear in copied spellbooks written long after their death, in handwriting that matches no living scribe.*

***Mordain Kest** was a warlord-exorcist of the late empire who bound **Monsters** into iron reliquaries, forced ghosts to testify in court, and is said to have sealed a dragon's shadow beneath what is now Deepwarden. Kest vanished during the Fall. Their reliquaries still surface in Ashland ruins, usually warm to the touch and never empty.*

***Edrava Salttide** ruled the southern salt-coast before the Fall. They fed their enemies to the tide, married four pirate-kings in succession, and paid druids to curse every harbour that refused their ships. Sailors who run the salt-coast at low winter tide still claim to see them counting ships that should have paid their toll. Now The Mire holds what the tide could not keep, and Edrava reigns as its bog witch and drowned queen, still counting and still collecting tolls no living hand can pay.*

***Old Wode of the Antlered Path** is the druid-name remembered in Greythorn's oldest tithe-songs. They are said to have walked into the standing stones at the end of the first post-Fall winter, struck the ground three times with an iron-shod staff, and returned with the agreement under which the forest accepts Greythorn's autumn tithe. The agreement has never been written down. The forest has never broken it.*

***Karnessa Iron-Vein** was a sorcerer whose blood was used to seal an Ashland vault that had begun to leak something through its walls. The vault has held. Karnessa's surviving line is said to be born with iron filings in their teeth and a tendency to bleed black under moonlight.*

***The Hollow Crown** is the title given to the last sovereign of the fallen empires. No personal name survives. Their statues have no faces. Their tomb has never been found. In the Ashlands the crown itself is said to hold court, black iron above an empty robe, and the legions still answer it. Some Ashland constructs still accept orders issued in the Hollow Crown's name. Others, less reassuringly, no longer do.*

***The Voice Beneath the Bells** appears in the chapel records of three different Bastions and the folk songs of all six. Every account mentions a child heard singing beneath a buried bell tower during the Fall of a city. No two accounts agree on the city, the song, or the bell. No grave has ever been found. Parties that descend into the deepest crypts are not always asked, on return, whether they heard anything. It is considered impolite.*

*The omens are smaller and more common.*

*A red moon over a Bastion means a debtor militia will march before dawn. White moths in winter mean a saint's relic has been disturbed. Three crows on a gallows mean the hanged will not stay down. A bell heard underground means something sealed has found a door. A road found dry during heavy rain is an imperial road and should not be followed after sunset. A corpse with clean fingernails has been dead before. A torch that burns blue near a ruin means magic is leaking. A torch that burns black means something is drinking the light.*

*These are not rules. They are warnings.*

*The lore of the Dying Lands provides names, scars, and old quarrels for expeditions, rival parties, patrons, **Monsters**, relics, and campaign goals. A scenario does not need to explain the whole world. It needs only enough history to make the blood on the ground feel older than the fight.*

### 1.4 What You Need to Play

To play Heraldry Skirmish, you need:

- **1–8 players**.
- One battlefield in either **Tabletop Mode** or **Grid Mode**.
  - **Tabletop Mode** uses an open **36"×36"** surface measured in inches, a suitable collection of terrain, and a tape measure.
  - **Grid Mode** uses a **36"×36"** battle map marked in **1"** squares.
- 1 miniature, standee, or token for each Hero, Hireling, Monster, and Summon in play.
- Distinguishable markers or miniatures for objectives, Treasure Chests, hazards, scenario elements, and other temporary battlefield features. Coins, paper tokens, spare miniatures, or similar markers are sufficient.
- A record sheet for each Hero and party, plus pencils or another method of recording game state.
- **AP**, **Activated**, **Resting**, **HP**, **NRG**, condition, and Luck tokens, or another method of tracking each resource and state.
- At least **4d4, 4d6, 4d8, 4d10, 2d12, and 2d20** dice.

### 1.5 Goals of the Game

A single game of Heraldry Skirmish is called an adventure. Your goal is to complete the scenario's objective and satisfy its victory conditions. Many competitive scenarios compare secured wealth, measured in **coins**. Throughout this book, values are written as **Xc**, where **X** is the number of coins. **Coin Value**, abbreviated **CV**, refers to an equivalent value in coins. Parties earn coins by looting treasure, completing objectives, defeating Monsters, and surviving long enough to escape the battlefield with their spoils.

#### 1.5.1 Campaign Goals and the Three Fates

In campaign play, the goal is **Triumph**.

In a competitive campaign, a party achieves **Triumph** when it completes any **5** different Stronghold Components. In a solo or cooperative campaign, a party achieves **Triumph** when it completes the rolled objective and extraction requirement in the **Triumph Finale**.

Over the course of a campaign, every Hero eventually meets one of three Fates:

- **Die:** A Hero who dies and is not returned to life before the next adventure is removed from the campaign permanently.
- **Retire:** A Hero may retire during the Town Phase. A retired Hero is removed from the Roster permanently, returns their eligible items to **Storage**, and adds a Retirement Payout to the Treasury. A Hero that retires at **Level 10** becomes a **Legendary Veteran**.
- **Triumph:** A Hero who remains on the Roster when their party achieves **Triumph** shares in that victory unless another rule says otherwise.

### 1.6 Rules Hierarchy and Precedence

If two rules conflict, use the more specific rule. Scenario rules override the core rules for that scenario. Class features, Powers, Monster rules, terrain rules, and item rules override the general rules they explicitly modify. If two rules are equally specific, use the more restrictive rule. Examples, summaries, and reference tables never override the main rules text.

For reading rules text, **must** marks a required instruction, **may** marks a permission or choice, and **cannot** marks a prohibition. These words do not create a separate precedence system: resolve every conflict using the rule-precedence paragraph above.

## 2. Core Mechanics

Heraldry Skirmish uses fixed procedures for uncertainty, movement, visibility, terrain, and resource spending. Uncertain actions use a **Check** against **12**. Unless a rule says otherwise, this section applies to every mode of play.

### 2.1 Core Terms

A **combatant** is any Hero, Hireling, Monster, Summon, or other model that can act on the battlefield.

A **Hero** is a player-controlled adventurer and the primary member of a party.

A **Hireling** is an allied non-Hero combatant whose profile or granting rule identifies them as a Hireling. Hirelings follow the normal rules for combatants unless a rule says otherwise.

A **Monster** is a neutral or hostile non-party combatant controlled by the Monster AI rules.

A **Summon** is a temporary combatant that their creating rule identifies as a Summon. A combatant does not become a Summon merely because a rule places or creates them. In particular, a named bestiary Monster placed by a Monster or scenario rule remains a **Monster** unless that rule explicitly identifies them as a Summon.

A **living combatant** is any combatant that does not have the **Undead** or **Construct** ability.

A **Celestial** is a combatant whose rule gives them the **Celestial** tag. A **Fiend** is a combatant whose rule gives them the **Fiend** tag; the **Fiend** Special Ability grants this tag. Neither tag has an effect by itself; rules that affect Celestials or Fiends say so explicitly.

An **allied** combatant is on your side. An **ally** is another combatant on your side; you are not your own ally. A rule that can affect you says **you**, **yourself**, **self**, or **you or an ally**. An **enemy** combatant is any combatant not on your side, including opposing party combatants and Monsters, unless a rule says a specific combatant is not an enemy for that interaction.

A **party** is one side's allied Heroes and Hirelings. Allied Summons belong to their controlling party for party-wide limits, but are not Heroes, Hirelings, or Roster members.

A **Party Leader** is the Hero designated by a side to anchor that side's Initiative rolls and to make choices assigned to the **Party Leader** by these rules. Each side designates one **Party Leader** as described in **6.1**. A party does not replace its **Party Leader** during an adventure. If the **Party Leader** is not on the battlefield, use **3.2** for Initiative and **6.1** for shared-control authority.

A **target** is the combatant, marker, hazard, terrain feature, or point chosen by a rule or action.

A combatant, marker, hazard, terrain feature, or point is **adjacent** to another when the horizontal distance and vertical separation between the two are each **1"** or less. In **Grid Mode**, the two horizontal positions must overlap or neighbour each other orthogonally or diagonally, and the vertical separation between them must be **1"** or less.

A **space** is the area a combatant, marker, hazard, or terrain feature occupies. A combatant's space is their rules **footprint**, determined by **Sz** under the **Size and Footprints** rules in **2.6**. In **Grid Mode**, it is the square or squares that footprint occupies.

Unless a rule says otherwise, combatants are aware in all directions and do not use facing.

An **Area of Effect** is any blast, burst, cone, line, Aura, or similar effect that affects an area rather than one target.

An **Explosion** is an effect that specifically says it explodes. Do not treat every Area of Effect as an Explosion unless the rule says so.

A combatant, marker, hazard, terrain feature, or point is **visible** to you if you have **LOS** to it, it is not **Hidden** from you, and no other rule prevents you from seeing it.

#### 2.1.1 Core Stats and Abbreviations

| Term      | Meaning                                                                              |
| --- | --- |
| **HP**    | Hit Points; a profile that lists one HP value uses it as both current and maximum HP unless a rule says otherwise |
| **AP**    | Action Points                                                                        |
| **NRG**   | Energy used to cast Powers or fuel abilities                                         |
| **AV**    | Armour Value                                                                         |
| **AD**    | Armour Dice rolled to generate **AV** |
| **CV**    | Coin Value used for rewards and extraction |
| **APL**   | Average Party Level                                                                  |
| **LVL**   | Monster Level |
| **LOS**   | Line of Sight                                                                        |
| **SPD**   | Speed, the distance moved per **Move** action |
| **Sz**    | Size: **S** (Small), **M** (Medium), **L** (Large), or **H** (Huge) |
| **TAP**   | Town Action Points used during campaign Town Phases                                  |

#### 2.1.2 Same-Named Effects

Two or more ongoing effects with the same name do not stack on the same combatant, item, or area unless a rule explicitly says otherwise. Apply only one instance at a time. Apply the instance with the strongest numerical effect. If tied, apply the one with the longest remaining duration. If the instances cannot be compared numerically, apply the most recently resolved instance. When the applied instance ends, another applicable instance may continue. Instantaneous effects resolve normally. Conditions use the stacking and immunity rules in **5.9 Conditions**.

**Bookkeeping aid:** When the source or expiry of an ongoing effect may matter later, players may place a token or note beside the affected model, item, or area showing those details. This is optional record-keeping only; the originating rule remains authoritative for the effect's duration, controller, stacking, and timing.

### 2.2 Ability Scores

Heroes and Hirelings use ability scores. A non-Monster Summon or other combatant uses the ability scores listed in their profile. If such a combatant must make a **STR**, **DEX**, **INT**, or **SPI Check** with an omitted score, treat that score as **+0** for that Check only; this does not grant an ability score for any other purpose. **Monsters never have or use ability scores.** Ability scores are added as modifiers to **Checks** and other listed rolls. Most starting Heroes have values between **-1** and **+3**.

Ability scores may be negative and have no maximum unless a rule says otherwise.

A combatant with ability scores has four ability scores:

- **Strength (STR):** melee force, physical power, climbing, forcing objects, and resisting bodily harm.
- **Dexterity (DEX):** ranged accuracy, speed, balance, stealth, dodging, and delicate physical tasks.
- **Intelligence (INT):** perception, reasoning, knowledge, investigation, initiative, **Arcane Spells**, and **Psychic Abilities**.
- **Spirit (SPI):** willpower, faith, resolve, leadership, and powers of faith, nature, and sorcery.

### 2.3 Ability Checks

When a rule calls for a **Check**, roll **1d20** and add the listed ability score. If the total is **12** or higher, the **Check** succeeds. If the total is **11** or lower, it fails.

The rule calling for the **Check** tells you which ability to use.

A **natural 1** on a d20 **Check** is a **Critical Failure** and always fails. A **natural 20** on a d20 **Check** is a **Critical Success** and always succeeds.

**Natural 1** and **natural 20** apply only to **d20 Checks** unless a rule says otherwise. Some attacks, Reactions, and Power rules define their own critical results for non-d20 rolls.

A **Monster** never makes a Check and has no **STR**, **DEX**, **INT**, or **SPI** score. If a rule would require a **Monster** to make a Check, do not roll it: resolve the normal failed-Check effect (not a **Critical Failure**) against that Monster automatically unless they are **Immune** to it. If a **Power** or scroll would require a **Monster** to make such a Check and that **Monster's LVL** is higher than the Level of the Hero using it, its **Casting Check** is made with **Disadvantage**.

The one exception is a **Terrain Check**: a Check required by the **Climb** or **Jump** rules, by a Terrain Type or **Terrain Tag**, or by a terrain feature or hazard marker that a scenario or Secondary Objective places. A **Monster** automatically succeeds on every **Terrain Check**. A Check that a Power, scroll, item, attack, Special Ability, or weather result requires directly is not a **Terrain Check**, even if that effect creates or alters terrain.

### 2.4 Advantages and Disadvantages

When a roll has **Advantage**, add one extra die of the affected type, then ignore the lowest single die of that type.

When a roll has **Disadvantage**, add one extra die of the affected type, then ignore the highest single die of that type.

For a **d20 Check**, the affected type is **d20**.

For a damage roll, only base damage dice are affected. After ignoring the required die, determine **Total Misses**, **Critical Hits**, exploding dice, and total damage using only the retained base damage dice.

For a non-d20 roll that uses more than one die type, the rule granting **Advantage** or **Disadvantage** determines the affected die type. If it does not, use the highest-sided die type in the roll.

If both **Advantage** and **Disadvantage** apply to the same roll, they cancel each other out, and the roll is made normally. Multiple instances of **Advantage** do not stack. Multiple instances of **Disadvantage** do not stack.

#### 2.4.1 Attack Advantage and Disadvantage

The following table lists every core rule that gives an attack **Advantage** or **Disadvantage**. Weapons, Talents, Powers, items, Monster abilities, terrain features, weather, injuries, scenarios, and other specific rules list any additional source in their own entries.

| Source | Attack Modifier | Full Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Attacker is at a **higher elevation** than the target | **Advantage** | **2.9.9** |
| Attacker resolves their first qualifying attack while **Hidden** | **Advantage** | **5.9** |
| Target is **Prone** | Melee attack: **Advantage** | **5.9** |
| Attacker is swimming in **Deep Water** | **Disadvantage** | **2.9.7** |
| Attacker is **Blinded** | **Disadvantage** | **5.9** |
| Attacker is **Frightened** by the target | **Disadvantage** | **5.9** |
| Attacker is **Weakened** | **Disadvantage** | **5.9** |
| Target has **Cover** | Ranged weapon attack, thrown weapon attack, or non-area damaging ranged Power: **Disadvantage** | **2.8.4** |
| Target is **Invisible**, and the attacker is adjacent but cannot ignore **Invisible** | **Disadvantage** | **5.9** |
| Target is **Prone** and the ranged weapon attacker is more than **2"** away | **Disadvantage** | **5.9** |
| Attack is a **Reflex Attack** | **Disadvantage** | **5.5.4** |
| Attack is the second or later weapon attack made by the same Hero or Hireling during one activation | **Disadvantage** | **5.7** |

These modifiers apply only to the roll stated by the rule. An extra base damage die, a flat modifier, or a reroll is not **Advantage** or **Disadvantage**.

This is not **Advantage** or **Disadvantage** and is listed here only to prevent confusion: an **Off-Hand Weapon** attack always rolls exactly **1** base damage die (**6.13**).

### 2.5 Action Points and Summons

Action Points (**AP**) measure how much a Hero, Hireling, allied Summon, or other player-controlled combatant can do in a round.

Heroes begin each round with **3 AP**. Hirelings begin each round with **2 AP**. Monsters do **not** use AP. Instead, when a **Monster** activates, resolve their activation entirely by following the Monster AI rules in **Section 9.5**.

Summons and other non-Monster combatants use the AP listed in their rules. An allied Summon with no listed AP has **2 AP**. A Summon created during a round gains their full listed or default AP immediately. If a combatant does not have enough AP to pay a cost, they cannot perform that action.

#### 2.5.1 Summon Limits

A party's limit is **2 allied Summons** in play.

If a rule would create a third allied Summon for that party, create the Summon, then immediately choose one allied Summon in that party to be dispelled and removed from play. Resolve the new Summon's "when summoned" effects only if the new Summon remains in play.

If more than one player controls that party, the player exercising **Party Leader** authority chooses which allied Summon is dispelled.

Enemy, neutral, and Monster-created Summons do not count against a party's allied Summon limit unless a rule says otherwise.

Unless a rule says otherwise, a **Summon** remains in play until they are reduced to **0 HP**, are dispelled through the allied Summon limit, are removed by a rule, or the adventure ends.

An allied Summon counts as a combatant under their party's command for activation order, AP economy, and Party Phase participation, but they do **not** count as a Hero or a Hireling for rules that reference those terms.

Unless a rule explicitly says otherwise, an allied **Summon** cannot take **Reactions**, cannot take the **Interact**, **Spot**, or **Hide** actions, cannot carry, claim, control, or score treasure or scenario objective markers, cannot contribute **Coin Value**, cannot satisfy extraction requirements, cannot complete campaign objectives, and is removed at the end of the adventure. If an allied **Summon** is carrying a treasure or scenario objective marker without a rule that allows them to do so, they immediately drop that marker in their current space.

A **Summon's** printed attack damage is complete; do not add an ability modifier unless that attack explicitly includes one.

### 2.6 Measurement, Size, Distances, and Rounding

You may measure any distance or check **LOS** at any time.

Heraldry Skirmish is played on a **36"×36"** battlefield unless a scenario says otherwise.

**Tabletop Mode:** Measure distances in inches between the closest points of the source and target spaces. If a rule measures from or to an origin point, target point, or other point, use that point.

**Grid Mode:** Use a **36"×36"** battle map marked in **1"** squares. A combatant occupies the squares listed by their **Sz** footprint. A marker, token, hazard, or terrain feature occupies every square whose centre lies under it, rounded outward at ties.

Each orthogonal square of movement or distance counts as **1"**, and each diagonal square counts as **1.5"**, unless a rule says otherwise. For range and other non-movement distances, count the shortest grid distance without counting the source square. Obstacles do not change this distance unless a rule says otherwise; check **LOS**, **Cover**, and terrain separately.

Track movement and distance in **0.5"** increments. Do not round a **1.5"** diagonal or a combatant's remaining movement.

If a source or target occupies more than one square, check each source-square and target-square pair. When range, **LOS**, and **Cover** apply to the same target or effect, one pair must satisfy all requirements. If more than one pair does, use the pair that grants the target the least **Cover**. If **Cover** is tied, use the shortest range. For a distance that does not also require **LOS** or **Cover**, use the closest occupied squares.

If a rule measures from or to a point, marker, hazard, or terrain feature, use the square containing it unless the rule says otherwise.

**Universal Rounding:** Do not round measured distances, listed fractional distances, or Grid Mode movement tracked in **0.5"** increments. When any other calculation in Heraldry Skirmish produces a fraction, round down to the nearest whole number immediately after that calculation. Rounding down is the default and need not be restated. A rule that requires a different direction must say so explicitly using the phrase **rounded up**.

**Minimum Values:** Except for ability scores, values cannot be reduced below **0** unless a rule explicitly says otherwise.

#### Size and Footprints

Every combatant has a **Size (Sz)**: **Small (S), Medium (M), Large (L),** or **Huge (H)**. Published profiles list **Sz** explicitly. If a temporary or generic combatant has no listed Size, treat them as **Medium (Sz M)**.

| Sz | Size | Footprint | Grid Footprint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **S** | Small | **1"×1"** | **1×1 square** |
| **M** | Medium | **1"×1"** | **1×1 square** |
| **L** | Large | **2"×2"** | **2×2 squares** |
| **H** | Huge | **3"×3"** | **3×3 squares** |

The listed footprint is authoritative for rules purposes even if a miniature uses a differently shaped or sized physical base. When needed, use a footprint template or marker beneath the miniature. Measure range, movement, **LOS**, Areas of Effect, terrain occupancy, adjacency, and overlap from the combatant's rules footprint. A combatant's entire footprint must fit in every legal final position.

Size grants no additional reach, damage, **AV**, resistance to forced movement, or other benefit unless another rule says so.

**Small:** A combatant with **Sz S** has the **Small** Special Ability. A combatant has **Small** if and only if their current Size is **Sz S**. A Small combatant cannot equip equipment with the **Heavy** trait. This restriction refers to the equipment trait, not the Monster Special Ability **Heavy**, which remains a separate rule. During voluntary movement, a Small combatant may move through spaces occupied by **Large** or **Huge** combatants, including enemies, but cannot end movement overlapping any combatant. This permission does not ignore terrain, hazards, movement costs, **Engagement**, **Reflex Attack**, or any other movement restriction.

**Changing Size:** When an effect changes a combatant's **Sz**, keep the centre of their footprint fixed. In **Grid Mode**, first identify the grid-aligned new footprints whose centres are nearest the old centre, ignoring obstructions. Choose a legal footprint only from those nearest placements; the controller chooses among legal ties, or use **9.5** for a Monster. If none is legal, the size-changing effect cannot resolve. In **Tabletop Mode**, the new footprint must fit legally at the fixed centre. When the effect ends, restore the previous Size using the same placement rule. If no such placement is legal, use the nearest legal placement instead, resolving ties by **Random Determination**. Changing Size never displaces another combatant.

#### 2.6.1 Declared Movement and Positional State

Before resolving voluntary movement or forced movement, declare the combatant's intended path and final position. Before resolving placement, declare only the final position unless the rule gives a path.

- **Tabletop Mode:** State the path, if any, and indicate the final position.
- **Grid Mode:** Declare the destination square and, if the path matters, each square entered. For a combatant that occupies more than one square, declare every destination square they will occupy.

An opposing player may measure and verify the declaration before movement or placement begins. In solo or cooperative play, verify it before movement or placement begins.

If the declaration is illegal, amend it or choose another action. An abandoned declaration costs no **AP**. If the declaration is legal, its path and final position are verified. Once movement begins, or once a **Reaction** is declared against that movement, the declaration cannot be amended or abandoned.

Resolve movement along the verified path. If a **Reaction** is triggered by that movement, resolve it at the first point on the path where its trigger occurs, before the combatant travels beyond that point. For that **Reaction** and its consequences, treat the moving combatant as occupying the trigger point.

If multiple **Reactions** trigger at different points on the same path, resolve them in path order. If multiple **Reactions** trigger at the same point, use **3.6 Timing Rules**.

After each **Reaction** or other effect that interrupts movement, continue the verified movement if the combatant remains able to do so and the remaining path is still legal. If the effect moves the combatant, leaves them unable to continue voluntary movement, or otherwise makes the remaining path illegal, end the movement at the combatant's current position. Do not refund any **AP** spent on that movement.

When movement or placement ends, its actual path and final position become the combatant's **Declared State**. A **Declared State** remains authoritative until the combatant moves, is moved, or a battlefield change invalidates it. Verify it before resolving a rule that depends on the combatant's position or path. If a miniature is moved accidentally, restore its **Declared State** before play continues; no roll or vote is required.

#### 2.6.2 Dice

Heraldry Skirmish uses the following dice: **d2, d3, d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, d20, and d100**.

- **d2:** Roll any die. Even results count as **2**, odd results count as **1**.
- **d3:** Roll a **d6**. Results of **1–2** count as **1**, **3–4** count as **2**, and **5–6** count as **3**.
- **d100:** Roll two **d10**, reading one as the tens digit and the other as the ones digit. A result of **0** on both dice counts as **100**. The **d100** is used only where a table lists a **d100** column or a rule explicitly calls for it.

#### 2.6.3 Random Determination

When a rule requires **1 random option** from a finite set and does not give another procedure, give every eligible option an equal chance. If only **1** option is eligible, use it without rolling. Otherwise, number the eligible options consecutively, then roll the smallest die listed in **2.6.2** that can include every option. For more than **100** options, roll enough **d10** digits to cover the highest option number, reading each **10** as **0**. Reroll **0** and any result greater than the number of eligible options.

### 2.7 Line of Sight and Areas of Effect

Most ranged attacks, Powers, and interactions require **Line of Sight (LOS)**.

#### 2.7.1 The Sight Line

Use one straight sight line between the source and target to determine both **LOS** and **Cover**.

**Tabletop Mode:** Draw the sight line from the centre of the source combatant's footprint, marker, hazard, terrain feature, or origin point to the centre of the target's footprint, marker, hazard, terrain feature, or target point.

**Grid Mode:** Draw the sight line from the centre of the source square to the centre of the target square.

If either occupies more than one Grid Mode square, use the same source-square and target-square pair for range, **LOS**, and **Cover**, as described in **2.6**. When **LOS** is checked together with range or **Cover**, one pair must satisfy every requirement under **2.6**. When **LOS** is checked alone, the source has **LOS** if at least one pair has an unblocked sight line.

Sight-line geometry is mutual: terrain or a combatant that blocks the line in one direction blocks it in both directions. A rule that changes an observer's senses, maximum **LOS**, visibility, or ability to draw **LOS** through terrain applies only to that observer unless it says otherwise.

Ignore the space the source occupies. Ignore weapons, banners, wings, scenic basing, and other decorative parts of a miniature unless a scenario or terrain rule says otherwise.

A combatant on a stable upper surface is not in the terrain supporting that surface. When drawing a sight line to or from that combatant, ignore only the part of the supporting feature directly beneath their footprint that the line touches as it leaves or reaches the combatant. Do not ignore the supporting surface if the sight line passes through it to reach something on the opposite side; such a sight line is blocked normally under **2.7.2**. Every other part of the feature applies normally.

**Hidden** and **Invisible** do not change the geometric sight line or block **LOS** by themselves. They change visibility and targeting as described in **2.8** and **5.9**.

#### 2.7.2 Blocked Line of Sight

**LOS** is blocked if the sight line crosses **Blocking Terrain**, or if a solid floor, roof, or platform lies between the source and target.

**Grid Mode:** **LOS** is also blocked if the sight line touches a corner shared by 2 **Blocking Terrain** squares.

**Cover Terrain** can be seen into and out of near its edge, but not across its depth.

**Tabletop Mode:** **LOS** is blocked if the sight line crosses **1"** or more of continuous **Cover Terrain** between the source and target spaces. Ignore **Cover Terrain** within the source and target spaces for this rule.

**Grid Mode:** **LOS** is blocked if the sight line passes through the interior of a **Cover Terrain** square that neither the source nor target occupies. A sight line that only touches the edge or corner of that square does not pass through it, but it does grant **Cover**.

If no legal sight line can be drawn, the target cannot be targeted by an **LOS**-based effect.

A rule that reduces a combatant's **LOS** to a stated distance sets a maximum sight range. It does not block **LOS** within that range.

#### 2.7.3 Areas of Effect

Areas of Effect cannot penetrate **Blocking Terrain** or a solid floor, roof, or platform. If the sight line from the origin point to a combatant, marker, hazard, terrain feature, or square is blocked by either under **2.7.2**, that target or square is unaffected, even if the template physically covers it. An Aura whose combatant source occupies more than one Grid Mode square uses every occupied source square, as described below.

Cover does not protect a combatant from an Area of Effect unless the effect or Cover rule says otherwise.

**Hidden** and **Invisible** do not prevent a combatant from being affected by an Area of Effect that does not target them directly.

| Shape | Area |
| --- | --- |
| **Cone X"** | A triangle extending **X"** from its origin along a chosen centreline, with a far edge **X"** wide and perpendicular to that centreline. |
| **Line X"** | A rectangle extending **X"** from its origin along a chosen centreline. Its default width is **1"**. |
| **Aura X"** | Extends **X"** in all directions from its source. Measure from a combatant's footprint in **Tabletop Mode** and every square they occupy in **Grid Mode**. For any other source, measure from its centre or listed origin point. Unless a rule says otherwise, an Aura moves with its source and ends when that source leaves play. |

Unless a rule says otherwise, a cone or line originates at the effect's source and does not affect the combatant it originates from. If a line lists a width but no length, its length equals the effect's **Range**.

A placed area's origin is the source, centre point, target point, marker, terrain feature, or other point named by its rule.

| Mode | Placing an Area |
| --- | --- |
| **Tabletop Mode** | Centre a placed square, rectangle, or circle on its origin point unless its rule says otherwise. Use its listed template, dimensions, or boundary. A square or rectangle may be oriented freely. |
| **Grid Mode** | Choose the origin square before measuring a cone, line, or placed area. Use the square containing the source or point named by the rule. If a source occupies more than one square, choose one legal occupied square. Measure a cone or line from that square's centre. Measure an Aura from every square its combatant source occupies, or from the single origin square of any other source. |

**Tabletop Mode:** If a combatant is the source of an Area of Effect other than an **Aura**, use the centre of their footprint as the origin point unless the rule names another origin point. A combatant is affected if any part of their rules footprint lies within or touches the area's boundary. A marker, hazard, or terrain feature is affected if any part of its rules space lies within or touches the area's boundary. A point is affected if it lies within or on that boundary.

In **Grid Mode**, Areas of Effect use geometric square-centre measurements rather than the orthogonal and diagonal distance counting in **2.6**, unless a rule says otherwise. Treat each grid square as **1"×1"** when measuring a shape. Determine affected squares as follows:

| Shape | Affected Squares |
| --- | --- |
| **Cone** | Every square whose centre lies within the cone, rounded outward at ties. |
| **Line** | Every square whose centre lies within its width, rounded outward at ties. Include the origin square if its centre lies within the line unless the rule says otherwise. |
| **Aura** | Every square whose centre lies within the listed straight-line distance of the centre of at least one source square, rounded outward at ties. Include every source square. |
| Square or rectangle | Exactly the listed number of squares along each dimension. The origin must be one of the central squares; the player resolving the effect chooses among tied central squares. |
| Other placed area | Every square whose centre lies within its boundary, rounded outward at ties. |

In **Grid Mode**, an Area of Effect cannot affect a square if the sight line from the centre of the origin square to the centre of that square is blocked by **Blocking Terrain** or a solid floor, roof, or platform under **2.7.2**, unless the rule says otherwise. An Aura with more than one source square affects the square if this sight line is unblocked from at least one source square.

Measure every Area of Effect in the horizontal plane. A difference in elevation between the origin and a combatant, marker, hazard, terrain feature, or square does not add distance and does not remove that target from the area, as described in **2.9.9**. A solid floor, roof, or platform lying between the origin and that target blocks the effect under **2.7.2**, so an Area of Effect does not reach a target separated from its origin by such a surface. Where no such surface lies between them, as at an open ledge, balcony, gantry, stair, or shaft, the area reaches every legal target within its horizontal footprint at every elevation.

A combatant, marker, hazard, or terrain feature that occupies more than one space is affected if at least one of those spaces is affected. Resolve the effect only once for each affected combatant, marker, hazard, or terrain feature unless the effect says otherwise.

Unless an Area of Effect says otherwise, roll its damage once and apply that same rolled total separately to every affected combatant. Whenever one damage roll is shared by multiple combatants, resolve it in this order:

1. Resolve target redirection, confirm affected combatants, then declare all **Reactions** to the source before rolling any damage dice, following **4.5**. Pay or commit their costs under **4.5**. Resolve declaration-triggered effects at their stated timings; retain declared defensive Reactions for step 4.
2. Roll the shared damage.
3. Before resolving any defence or mitigation, resolve any **Luck** reroll under **2.10**. The **Luck** window closes when defence or mitigation begins.
4. Using the final roll, each affected combatant resolves their defensive **Reaction** declared in step 1, if any, then applies **AD**, **AV**, **Resistant**, **Vulnerable**, **Immune**, and other mitigation under **5.1.1**. No new Reaction may be declared to this source. If resolution order matters, use **3.6 Timing Rules**.

A non-area effect with multiple targets or separate damage instances rolls damage separately for each target or damage instance unless it says one roll is shared. Powers use the shared-expression default in **8.2**.

### 2.8 Cover, Light, Hidden, and Visibility

Concealment in Heraldry is a ladder of three steps. Each step is harder to reach than the one below it and gives more protection.

| Step | State | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Exposed** | The combatant has no **Cover**. Attacks and effects target them normally. |
| 2 | **Cover** | The combatant is still targeted normally, but applicable ranged attacks and effects against them suffer **Disadvantage**. |
| 3 | **Hidden** | The combatant cannot be targeted by anything that requires **LOS**. |

**Cover** is the gateway to **Hidden**: a combatant becomes **Hidden** only by holding **Cover** from every enemy that has **LOS** to them, or by standing outside every enemy's **LOS** entirely. A combatant who loses **Cover** falls to step 1 and loses **Hidden** with it.

To close on a concealed enemy, an attacker has three answers: move within their **Hide distance**, use **Spot**, or break their **Cover** by changing the angle of approach. **Areas of Effect** are the exception at every step, because an area that does not target a combatant directly still affects them.

#### 2.8.1 Visibility State

Each battlefield has one **Visibility State**:

- **Light**
- **Darkness**

If a scenario, weather result, or special rule does not set the battlefield's **Visibility State**, the battlefield starts in **Light**.

#### 2.8.2 Light

**Light** has no special effect unless a rule says otherwise.

A **Light Source** is a torch, lantern, brazier, campfire, magical light, glowing terrain feature, or similar source of illumination. Unless a rule lists another size, it has **Aura 3"**. A carried **Light Source** uses its carrier as its source.

A **Light Source** creates **Light** within its **Aura**, removing **Darkness** there but not any other source of **Cover**.

A combatant carrying a **Light Source** cannot be **Hidden** unless a rule says otherwise.

A **Light Source** **Aura** follows the Area of Effect geometry and obstruction rules in **2.7.3**. It is not a harmful effect unless a rule says otherwise.

#### 2.8.3 Darkness

**Darkness** provides **Cover** to a combatant in its area against nonadjacent enemies, as described in **2.8.4**. While the battlefield's **Visibility State** is **Darkness**, every area not lit by a **Light Source** is in **Darkness**. A rule may instead create **Darkness** only within a specific area.

**Magical Darkness** is **Darkness** that a rule explicitly describes as magical. Ordinary **Darkvision** does not ignore **Cover** or visual penalties caused by **Magical Darkness** unless another rule says otherwise. All other **Darkness** is nonmagical **Darkness**.

#### 2.8.4 Cover

An area that provides **Cover** does not change its underlying **Terrain Type**, **Terrain Tags**, movement, hazards, or **LOS** unless its rule says otherwise.

A combatant has **Cover** from an enemy when at least one of the following is true:

- the enemy is not adjacent, and the target occupies **Cover Terrain** or an area that provides **Cover**;
- the sight line between them crosses, or touches the edge or corner of, a terrain feature that is not **Open Terrain**, outside their own spaces;
- the sight line between them crosses another combatant that is not **Prone** or **Knocked Out** and whose **Sz** is the same as or larger than the target's **Sz**;
- a rule says the combatant has **Cover**.

For a target combatant that occupies more than one square in **Grid Mode**, determine whether they occupy **Cover Terrain** using the target square selected under **2.6**.

**Cover** is binary. Multiple sources of **Cover** do not stack unless a rule says otherwise.

*Example: a Ranger has clear **LOS** to a Skeleton Warrior, but the sight line crosses their own Fighter. The Skeleton Warrior has **Cover**, so the Ranger rolls their base damage dice with **Disadvantage**. The Fighter is not a target and suffers nothing. If the Ranger first spends **1 AP** to **Shift** clear of the sight line, no **Cover** applies.*

If a rule lets a combatant ignore **Cover** from a source, that source provides no **Cover** against them. If a rule only lets a combatant draw **LOS** through terrain or a visibility effect, it does not block their **LOS**, but it still provides **Cover** unless that rule says otherwise.

**Cover** is not the same as **Hidden** or **Invisible**. **Cover** granted only by a sight line crossing a combatant does not satisfy any requirement to have **Cover** in order to become or remain **Hidden**.

If a target has **Cover**, ranged weapon attacks and thrown weapon attacks against them roll their base damage dice with **Disadvantage**. If a non-area damaging ranged Power rolls base damage dice against a target in **Cover**, roll its base damage dice with **Disadvantage**. **Cover** gives **Disadvantage** to harmful **LOS**-based Power **Checks** made by the caster against the covered target. **Cover** does not modify **Checks** made by the target unless the Power says otherwise. **Cover** never applies to melee weapon attacks.

Areas of Effect and hazards ignore **Cover** unless a rule says otherwise.

#### 2.8.5 Hidden and Invisible

**Hidden** and **Invisible** are separate conditions. A combatant may have either or both. Neither blocks **LOS**; each limits visibility and targeting as described in **5.9**.

While a combatant has both conditions, **Invisible** governs targeting, and the combatant does not gain the **Hidden** benefit in **5.9** until **Invisible** ends. The combatant remains **Hidden** for every other rule. **Spot** removes only **Hidden** unless a rule says otherwise.

If a rule explicitly removes **Hidden** or **Invisible** from a combatant, that combatant cannot regain the removed condition until the end of the round unless a more specific rule says otherwise. Losing **Hidden** or **Invisible** through the ordinary end conditions in **5.9** does not trigger this restriction.

### 2.9 Terrain

Every terrain feature, distinct part of a complex feature, and supporting surface has exactly one **Terrain Type** and any number of **Terrain Tags**.
